Intel Just Dropped 10% in a Week. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©TIKR
Key Takeaways

Intel stock fell 10% in the week through Thursday's close, mostly in a chip selloff after Lam Research said supply chain constraints held back its outlook.

TSMC's offer to back customers short of Intel's packaging capacity was Intel's one worry of its own, and nothing last week cut Intel's guidance or estimates.

Intel trades at 51x forward earnings, right at its five-year average, and the $117 consensus target is 35% above Friday's close.

For investors who believe in the foundry turnaround, the drop looks like a chance to buy, and Intel's Oct. 29 third-quarter report has to back it up.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) stock fell 10% in the week through Thursday's close, while the Nasdaq 100 dropped 3%. Friday's 1.7% bounce to $87 leaves it up 136% in 2026. So, time to lock in those gains… or buy more?

Lam's warning hit the whole chip group

Most of the damage came Thursday, after Lam Research (LRCX:NASDAQ) guided to $8.6 billion of December-quarter revenue at the midpoint. Its CFO, Doug Bettinger, said on the call that guidance "would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints."

That revived AI spending fears, and chip stocks sold off across the board. Intel had no news of its own.

But read Bettinger's line again: Lam's demand is outrunning its supply, and so is Intel's. And on its second-quarter call, management said it would fall short of demand again in the fourth quarter

TSMC wants Intel's packaging customers

Intel's own worry came from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE). On Oct. 15, CEO C.C. Wei said TSMC would back customers short of Intel's EMIB-T packaging capacity.

Packaging is the first foundry business Intel expects to ramp. CFO David Zinsner sees revenue picking up in the second half of 2027, at a gross margin of around 40%. Intel hasn't named a customer yet, and TSMC's pitch could squeeze pricing. Nor has it said whether the fatal Oct. 14 blast at its Kiryat Gat plant in Israel cut production.

Key Takeaways

Visa gained 13% and Mastercard 12% in the past month (through Friday's close), while the Nasdaq 100 fell 6%.

Neither company has reported new results during the run, so both look like holds until they do.

Mastercard's forward P/E has climbed from 23.3x in June to 29.3x, just under its five-year average of 31.0x, and the mean analyst target is only 8% above Friday's close.

Visa reports on Oct. 27 and Mastercard on Oct. 29, and Mastercard has guided to full-year revenue growth at the high end of the low double digits.

Visa (V:NYSE) gained 13% and Mastercard (MA:NYSE) 12% in the past month (through Friday's close), while the S&P 500 slipped 1% and the Nasdaq 100 fell 6%. Mastercard set a record close on Thursday, then gave back 1.5% on Friday.

Neither company has reported a quarter since late July. So the run mostly reflects where investors are moving their money.

Chips out, card swipes in

As AI chip stocks sold off, investors went looking for steadier growth, and card swipes fit the bill. Both networks set records along the way.

Mastercard also gave the rally a story of its own. On Oct. 15, it launched its Global Money Platform with BVNK, the stablecoin company it bought in August for up to $1.8 billion. Businesses get one connection for regular currencies and stablecoins alike. The platform also offers stablecoin-linked cards in more than 130 countries, with payouts in more than 40 currencies planned for 2027.

Visa moved the same day, taking stablecoin funding on Visa Direct from a pilot to commercial use.

Mastercard hasn't said what the platform will earn, and real revenue is likely years away. Still, it plugs into the part of the business that's already growing fastest. Value-added services rose 18% in the second quarter, against 8% for the payment network.

title: US Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Federal Reserve Decision and Major Technology Earnings
detail:
US Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Federal Reserve Decision and Major Technology Earnings
Fiona Craig
Mon, October 26, 2026 at 7:42 AM EDT 6 min read
^GSPC
^DJI
^IXIC
^NDX
Nasdaq sign on a tall building ©Dries Buytaert

US stock index futures advanced on Monday following two consecutive weeks of declines for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, as investors prepared for a Federal Reserve interest rate decision and quarterly earnings from several major technology companies.

At 06:06 ET (10:06 GMT), S&P 500 futures were up 23 points, or 0.3%, while Nasdaq 100 futures gained 79 points, also rising 0.3%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures advanced 245 points, equivalent to 0.5%.

The gains followed selling pressure in technology and artificial intelligence-related shares, driven partly by concerns about borrowing costs and the financing of large infrastructure investments.

Market attention is now turning to the Federal Reserve's two-day policy meeting, beginning Tuesday, alongside economic data and corporate earnings announcements scheduled throughout the week.

Technology Shares Weigh on US Equity Markets

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite have recorded two consecutive weeks of losses, with technology companies accounting for a substantial portion of the declines.

Investors have been reassessing valuations across businesses exposed to artificial intelligence, particularly those undertaking large capital expenditure programmes.

Concerns have centred on the amount of debt being used to finance AI infrastructure and the potential effects of elevated interest rates on investment returns.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average performed differently during the period, supported by buying interest in sectors including healthcare, utilities and industrials.

These sectors attracted investment as market participants adjusted their exposure to technology companies.

Monday's increase in equity futures indicated a partial recovery ahead of several events that could influence expectations for corporate profitability and monetary policy.

Federal Reserve Expected to Hold Interest Rates

The Federal Reserve is scheduled to begin its two-day monetary policy meeting on Tuesday, with an interest rate announcement expected on Wednesday.

Market participants widely anticipate that the central bank will leave borrowing costs unchanged following its September decision to increase rates for the first time since 2023.

Federal Reserve officials have continued to emphasise the objective of returning inflation to the central bank's 2% target.

However, some policymakers have indicated that an immediate additional rate increase may not be necessary.

As a result, investors will be monitoring comments from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh following the policy announcement.

Analysts at Deutsche Bank said the central bank could maintain a restrictive policy outlook even if it decides against raising rates at the forthcoming meeting.

"The overall message is still likely to favour tighter monetary policy. Our economists believe recent inflation figures support further rate increases over time, even if the Fed leaves rates unchanged this week," the analysts wrote.

According to CME's FedWatch Tool, market pricing indicated approximately a 73% probability of another interest rate increase at the Federal Open Market Committee's final meeting of the year in December.

The probability reflects market expectations at the time of the report and may change as new economic information becomes available.

US GDP and Inflation Data Could Influence Rate Expectations

Investors will also receive economic indicators that could affect expectations for future Federal Reserve decisions.

An advance estimate of third-quarter US gross domestic product is scheduled for release during the week.

The report will provide information about the pace of economic activity and the contributions of household spending, business investment and other components of output.

September's personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index is also due.

The PCE index is the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation and will provide updated information about price developments.

The central bank will assess these figures alongside labour market conditions and other economic indicators when considering future monetary policy adjustments.

Verizon, Visa and Major Technology Companies Prepare to Report

Corporate earnings will form another major part of the week's financial market calendar.

Verizon Communications (NYSE:VZ) and Welltower (NYSE:WELL) are scheduled to publish their quarterly results on Monday.

On Tuesday, Visa (NYSE:V), Boeing (NYSE:BA) and Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO) are among the largest companies expected to report.

Technology earnings will become a particular focus later in the week.

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) are scheduled to announce results on Wednesday, followed by Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) on Thursday.

The reports will provide information about revenue growth, operating profitability, cash flow and capital expenditure plans.

Investors will pay particular attention to spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure and the extent to which those investments are contributing to business performance.

Recent concerns have focused on the combination of substantial infrastructure commitments, increasing debt and elevated financing costs.

The earnings announcements could provide additional information about how major technology companies are managing these factors.

Oil Prices Decline Amid US-Iran Diplomatic Efforts

Oil prices moved lower on Monday following reports of diplomatic activity involving Qatar, Iran and the United States.

Qatari mediators reportedly travelled to Tehran over the weekend to explore possible measures to reduce tensions between Iran and Washington.

The discussions followed reports that US President Donald Trump was considering further military action against Iran after the November midterm elections.

Speaking to Fox News on Sunday, Trump said it was "approaching the point when a decision must be made" about whether to conduct additional strikes or pursue an agreement with Tehran.

Iranian officials had previously warned of retaliatory measures in response to further military action.

Regional tensions have also been affected by exchanges of attacks involving Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

These developments have raised concerns about potential interruptions to oil production and transportation in the Middle East.

The decline in crude prices on Monday followed reports of diplomatic efforts, although the possibility of further disruption remained relevant to energy market expectations.

Analysts Anticipate Continued Market Volatility

Analysts at Neuberger said the combination of corporate earnings, monetary policy decisions and political developments could contribute to further fluctuations in financial markets.

In a research note, the analysts said the coming weeks could bring "volatility" as third-quarter earnings, the Federal Reserve meeting and the US midterm elections occur against an "already unstable environment".

The assessment reflects the number of developments that investors will be monitoring over the coming weeks.

Corporate earnings will provide information about business performance and investment spending, while the Federal Reserve's announcement will influence expectations for borrowing costs.

Economic data, geopolitical developments and the approaching US elections will provide additional considerations for market participants.

Monday's gains in stock index futures marked an initial recovery following recent declines, ahead of the scheduled announcements.

Meanwhile, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News on Sunday that the US and Canada are "very close" to finalizing a trade deal as talks are "gathering steam." In August, Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on roughly US$20 billion worth of American goods, matching Washington's move "dollar for dollar" as trade tensions between the two nations escalated.

Monday's economic calendar has the Chicago Fed national activity index for September at 8:30 am ET, followed by the Dallas Fed manufacturing survey for October at 10:30 am.

Spot gold nudged 0.6% higher to $4,030 per troy ounce, while bitcoin dipped 0.2% to $80,336.

title: Strategy Just Dropped 13% in a Month. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up?
detail:
Strategy Just Dropped 13% in a Month. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up?
Gian Estrada

BTC-USD
^NDX

Strategy Just Dropped 13% in a Month. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©Dean Drobot via Canva
Key Takeaways

Strategy stock has fallen 13% since Sept. 22 (through Friday's close), most of it on Oct. 16, after MSCI's new rule put Strategy's place in its global indexes at risk.

Funds tracking MSCI hold only about 13 million shares, but the rule threatens the premium Strategy needs to keep selling stock for bitcoin.

Strategy bought just over 500 bitcoin in two weeks while putting more than $190 million a week into repurchases of its STRC preferred stock.

Third-quarter results on Oct. 29 and MSCI's Nov. 11 list come next, and the list is worth waiting for before buying more.

Strategy (MSTR:NASDAQ) stock is down 13% since Sept. 22 (through Friday's close), more than twice the Nasdaq 100's 6% drop. Most of that came the day after MSCI (MSCI:NYSE) changed who qualifies for its indexes, and bitcoin's slide did the rest.

Bitcoin's slide, with leverage on top

Bitcoin fell below $84,000 on Oct. 7 in a wave of leveraged selling, then slid again on Oct. 14 after a hotter-than-expected inflation report. Strategy went down with it, as did crypto stocks in general (Coinbase (COIN:NASDAQ) fell 16% over the month).

The stock moves harder than the coin, both ways. When the OCC finalized its GENIUS Act stablecoin rules on Oct. 21, bitcoin rose about 3% and Strategy rose roughly three times as much.

That's leverage at work: debt and preferred stock sit ahead of common shareholders, and the premium investors pay swings on top. Strategy's total debt went from $2.25 billion in fiscal 2023 to $8.25 billion in fiscal 2025…

MSTR Total Debt vs. Cash and Short-Term Investments: Fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)
MSCI hit the premium

On the evening of Oct. 15, MSCI adopted a rule that makes non-operating companies ineligible for its global indexes. Strategy fell 10% the next day, even with bitcoin up that morning. MSCI will name the companies it hits on Nov. 11, and the rule kicks in at the Nov. 30 close.

TIKR tracks 16 analysts on Strategy. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Strategy, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Strategy's Analyst Ratings

The forced selling is small: funds tracking MSCI hold about 13 million shares, less than a day's volume. The premium takes the bigger hit. Strategy grows the bitcoin value behind each share, net of its debt and preferred stock, by selling common stock above that net value and buying more bitcoin. Its gauge for that cushion, mNAV (the share price divided by net bitcoin value per share), was only about 1.07x in August. Without index funds as reliable buyers, a premium that thin is harder to win back.

And it's the whole pitch. As Strategy founder and executive chairman Michael Saylor said on Bloomberg Talks on Oct. 13: "you should buy the digital equity of a company like MSTR or Strive and you can expect to outperform Bitcoin because we're able to amplify our Bitcoin per share with our digital credit."

Selling stock has paid for that. Diluted shares nearly tripled from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2025, and the count has kept climbing this year…

MSTR Diluted Shares Outstanding: Fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)
The bitcoin buying has slowed to a trickle

Strategy raised just $21 million from common stock in the week to Oct. 11, enough for 250 bitcoin. Over those same seven days, it bought back $192.4 million of its STRC preferred stock.

The next week, it bought 267 bitcoin for $22.1 million and spent $193.1 million more on STRC, and on Oct. 19 its board added $1 billion to the buyback. Over those two weeks, Strategy put about nine times as much into its preferred stock as into bitcoin, all while Saylor was telling Bloomberg that bitcoin's bull market is just beginning.

I'd wait for Nov. 11

Three dates come first: Oct. 28, when shareholders vote on paying preferred dividends daily; Oct. 29, when third-quarter results land after the bell (with an estimated $20.91 billion digital-asset gain already disclosed); and Nov. 11, when MSCI publishes its list.

Analysts still see plenty of upside: the consensus target was $239 on Oct. 16, 64% above Friday's close, though down from $560 a year earlier…

MSTR Stock Mean Price Target: 1-Year (TIKR)

Cantor Fitzgerald raised its target to $208 from $186 on Oct. 16, and its target rests mostly on bitcoin reaching $112,000 within 12 months.

Personally, I wouldn't sell over one index rule and bitcoin's swings, but I wouldn't load up before Nov. 11 either. Until the list is out, Strategy is just bitcoin with leverage.

Of course, if mNAV holds above 1x even with Strategy on the list, stock sales that fund bitcoin purchases would keep adding net bitcoin value per share, and the leverage that hurt this month could start working for it.

Meta fell 7% as AI spending outran its cash flow, and MetLife's Drew Matus says investors punish spending cuts too.

Meta beat revenue estimates, with sales up 26%. Yet third-quarter capital expenditure (capex) of $34.9 billion topped operating cash flow, and shares fell on Oct. 22.

What Do Investors Actually Want From AI Spending?

Four more tech giants face the same test after Meta's selloff. Microsoft and Alphabet report Wednesday, followed by Amazon and Intel on Thursday.

Bloomberg's hosts said the four make up about 15% of the Nasdaq 100, which has fallen roughly 7% this month.

Matus said firms that cut capex get punished. Firms that raise it get the same treatment.

"I don't actually really know what people want from these people."

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OT_EussjmW0

Investors want proof that AI supports long-term growth, he said, yet debates over jobs and profits will persist.

Meta also announced a new class of nonvoting Class C stock. Scotiabank noted that management indicated an equity raise may be necessary.

Alphabet fell about 4% after hours in July when it lifted capex guidance. BeInCrypto's filing review found AI capex draining cash at Microsoft and Amazon.

Can Big Tech Spend as Much as It Promises?

Matus doubted that headline budgets will turn into spending this year, since firms must find workers, equipment and land first.

However, he said industries most exposed to AI are hiring more people, not fewer.

The Federal Reserve (Fed) meets Oct. 27 and 28 in a packed Fed week. Its decision lands Wednesday afternoon, hours before Microsoft and Alphabet are due to report.

The Fed raised rates in September to a 3.75% to 4% range. Traders scaled back October hike bets after Chair Kevin Warsh said hotter inflation had not changed his view.

Matus expects Warsh to skip a move and revisit policy in December.

Matus argues AI drives capex, equity gains and consumer spending at once. He called that economic concentration more worrying than the stock market's.

One weak outlook from a single company could therefore test that whole chain.

(Bloomberg) -- US stock futures advanced and crude oil retreated as traders weighed the latest geopolitical developments over Iran and looked ahead to a string of central bank rate decisions this week.

Bitcoin Billionaires Are Racing to Ride a 3,000% Crypto Boom

Trump Says Decision Nearing on Iran: Deal or 'Finish It Off'

Nasdaq 100 futures climbed 0.6%, while contracts on the S&P 500 gained 0.4% after the benchmark fell Friday. Brent dropped over 1% to around $115 a barrel, pulling back from its highest close since April. President Donald Trump said it's "getting to be decision time" on whether to reach a deal with Tehran or resume attacks as threats from Iran and the Houthis against Americans in the Middle East mount.

Asian stocks looked set for a mixed start, with gains in US futures offering some support while recent weakness in technology shares weighed. A gauge of chipmakers last week posted its longest run of weekly losses since November, leaving the durability of any rebound in the artificial intelligence trade in view.

The dollar was broadly steady against its Group-of-10 peers on Monday after ending last week lower. Treasuries had given back some of their earlier gains on Friday as US technology stocks and French bonds stabilized. The euro was quoted higher early Monday after France dodged a downgrade at Moody's Ratings.

Investors face a pivotal stretch as renewed geopolitical tensions, stubborn inflation and cracks in the artificial intelligence trade test risk appetite heading into November. Central-bank decisions in the US, euro zone and Japan this week will provide the next test, with policymakers balancing the threat of higher energy costs against signs of strain across financial markets.

"We stay tactically risk-off until mid-Nov," Michael Hartnett, strategist at Bank of America Corp., wrote in a note to clients. "Expect down-in-yields, down-in-stocks, down-in US dollar trade."

The Federal Reserve raised rates in September for the first time since 2023 and signaled another increase was likely this year. While US inflation has remained elevated, officials have indicated little urgency to move again this week, with economists and investors expecting the next increase in December.

Geopolitical risks are also likely to remain elevated heading into next month. Trump has suggested US strikes on Iran could resume after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while officials have warned the period between the vote and the new Congress taking office could be particularly dangerous.

Key Takeaways

Meta stock fell about 9% in the past week (through Friday's close). Most of the drop came after a third-quarter report that showed 26% revenue growth and negative free cash flow.

The ad business is still growing fast, and the selling is about how Meta pays for AI, including a new non-voting Class C stock that is partly for raising capital.

A $25 billion New Mexico fine adds to the quarter's $9.89 billion legal charge, though Meta's cash covers the fine several times over.

After the drop, Meta trades below its usual forward multiple, which makes it a buy for investors who can live with some dilution.

Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) is down about 9% over the past week (through Friday's close). Most of that came after a third-quarter report that was strong everywhere except cash. (The Nasdaq 100 fell just 2%.)

Ads grew 26%, and that wasn't enough

Revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, ahead of the $63.41 billion analysts expected. Without a $9.89 billion legal charge, earnings per share would have been $7.40, against $6.80 expected. And fourth-quarter guidance of $73 billion to $76 billion has a midpoint above consensus.

But CFO Susan Li gave no 2027 budget. She said Meta plans "to continue investing aggressively to support both our core business and emerging AI initiatives."

The AI bill is coming due

Third-quarter capex hit $34.91 billion, above the $32.79 billion of operating cash flow. That left free cash flow at negative $2.12 billion. It's been building for years: capex took about 60% of operating cash flow in 2025, up from 32% in 2021…

Meta Platforms (META): cash from operations vs. capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

…and Meta just raised the floor of its 2026 capex range to $135 billion. On top of that, Meta had $454.5 billion of non-cancelable contractual commitments as of Sept. 30.

Then there's a new non-voting Class C stock, arriving in January 2027. It's partly for raising capital. Meta has looked like the AI spender that doesn't need outside money, unlike OpenAI. If it does sell new shares, the spending has to earn its keep. And on Thursday, Meta's credit default swaps hit a record high.

Plus: the day Meta reported, a New Mexico court ordered it to pay $25 billion over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Interest runs at 15% a year. Meta says it will win on appeal. Even if it doesn't, its $82.5 billion of cash covers the fine more than three times over.
